name: Americana from Scarf Hold Position
description: Master the Americana shoulder lock from Scarf Hold Position. Learn figure-four grip setup, perpendicular finishing angle, and safe application from kesa gatame.
summary: The Americana from Scarf Hold Position is a figure-four shoulder lock applied from kesa gatame, using the top player's perpendicular seating angle to rotate the trapped near arm and torque the opponent's glenohumeral joint until they tap.
target_area: Shoulder joint (specifically glenohumeral joint and rotator cuff)
overview:
Within the americana family, the scarf hold entry occupies a distinct niche because kesa gatame already supplies the head-and-arm control that other variants must first establish. Unlike the Americana from mount or side control, this variant positions the attacker's hands near the target wrist from the outset, shortening the path to the figure-four. The perpendicular seating angle generates rotational leverage on the glenohumeral joint through body mechanics rather than pure arm strength, making this one of the highest-percentage americana setups in grappling.

From the scarf hold, the attacker transitions from head control to wrist control while maintaining crushing hip pressure against the opponent's ribcage. The figure-four grip is established with the near arm securing the wrist and the far arm threading behind it, creating the classic paint brush finishing motion. The perpendicular angle means the attacker can use their entire torso rotation to drive the wrist toward the mat, applying substantially more force than arm-based finishes from parallel positions.

Defensively, the bottom player must recognize the grip transition early and fight to straighten their arm before the figure-four locks in. Once the figure-four is secured with the elbow pinned, escape becomes extremely difficult. The scarf hold Americana represents a fundamental submission that rewards patience, grip precision, and understanding of rotational shoulder mechanics over explosive athleticism.

injury_risks.injury: Rotator cuff tear (supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor)
injury_risks.recovery_time: 3-6 months with physical therapy, possible surgical intervention

injury_risks.injury: Shoulder capsule damage and labral tears

injury_risks.recovery_time: 3-6 months, high risk of chronic instability
4-8 weeks for strain, 3-4 months for tear

safety_considerations.application_speed: SLOW and progressive - 3-5 seconds minimum from initial pressure to expected tap. In drilling, apply 10-20% pressure maximum.
tap_signals: Verbal tap (saying 'tap' or any verbal signal)
Physical hand tap on opponent or mat (minimum 2 taps)
Physical foot tap on mat or opponent
Any distress vocalization or unusual sound
Slapping mat with free hand repeatedly
release_protocol: Immediately stop all rotational pressure on the shoulder
Release the figure-four grip on the wrist
Carefully lower the arm back to neutral position (do not drop suddenly)
Release control of the elbow and allow opponent to move freely
Check with partner verbally to ensure they are okay
If partner indicates pain, encourage them to keep shoulder mobile and seek medical attention if pain persists
training_restrictions: Never spike, jerk, or apply sudden rotational force
Never use competition speed or full pressure in training
Always allow clear access to tap with free hand
Stop immediately at any sign of discomfort (do not wait for tap in drilling)
Never practice on partners with existing shoulder injuries without explicit permission and medical clearance
Avoid repeated submissions on the same shoulder in a single training session

attacker.name: from Scarf Hold Position Attacker
attacker.description: Learn to attack with the Americana from Scarf Hold. Step-by-step figure-four grip mechanics, paint brush finish, and counters to common defensive responses.
attacker.overview: The Americana from Scarf Hold Position exploits the perpendicular angle unique to kesa gatame to isolate and attack the near arm with a figure-four shoulder lock. The scarf hold configuration provides natural wrist and elbow control through existing head-and-arm control, making the transition to americana grip seamless compared to other starting positions. Your hip pressure pins the opponent's torso while the perpendicular angle generates superior rotational leverage on the shoulder joint, creating one of the highest-percentage americana finishes available. The key to success is the controlled grip transition from head control to wrist control without sacrificing positional dominance.
key_principles: Control the wrist with your head-control hand before releasing the head, maintaining constant connection throughout the grip transition
Pin the opponent's elbow to the mat as the fulcrum point before applying any rotational pressure on the shoulder
Use hip pressure and chest connection to prevent the opponent from turning into you during the lock application
Apply the figure-four with your forearm positioned behind the opponent's wrist, not their hand, to maximize rotational control
Drive the wrist toward the mat using torso rotation and body weight rather than arm strength alone
Maintain patient, progressive pressure throughout the finish - the perpendicular angle provides mechanical advantage that eliminates the need for explosive force
setup_requirements: Established scarf hold with secure head control and near arm trapped across your body
Opponent's near arm accessible and bent at approximately 90 degrees, not tucked tight against their body
Hip pressure consolidated against opponent's ribcage with low base preventing bridge escapes
Far arm (head control arm) positioned to transition smoothly to wrist control without creating space
Opponent's far arm accounted for to prevent frame creation during grip transition

execution_steps.description: Ensure your hips are heavy against the opponent's ribcage with your near arm threading under their trapped arm. Confirm head control is tight with your far arm wrapped around their head. Your chest should be pressing into their upper body with no space between your torso and theirs.
execution_steps.timing: 2-5 seconds to verify all control points

execution_steps.action: Transition head control hand to wrist
execution_steps.description: Release your far arm from around the opponent's head and immediately slide it down to grip their near-side wrist. Pin the wrist firmly to the mat beside their hip. This transition must be smooth and fast to prevent the opponent from extracting their arm or establishing defensive frames during the brief moment without head control.

execution_steps.action: Pin the elbow to the mat
execution_steps.description: Use your near arm to control the opponent's elbow, pressing it firmly against the mat. The elbow becomes the fulcrum point for the entire submission. Ensure the arm is bent at approximately 90 degrees with the forearm pointing upward. If the arm is too straight, use your chest pressure to walk the elbow closer to their body.

Thread your far arm (the one controlling the wrist) underneath the opponent's forearm so your forearm sits behind their wrist. Grip your own wrist or forearm with your near hand, creating the classic figure-four configuration. Ensure the grip is tight with no slack between your forearm and the back of their wrist.

execution_steps.action: Adjust body angle for maximum leverage
execution_steps.description: Shift your hip pressure slightly toward the opponent's head to load weight over the trapped shoulder. Your perpendicular angle should create a direct line of force from your torso rotation through the figure-four into their shoulder joint. Keep your base wide with your back leg extended to prevent being rolled during the finish.

Slowly rotate the opponent's wrist toward the mat in an arc motion, keeping their elbow pinned as the stationary fulcrum. Use your entire torso to drive the rotation rather than pulling with your arms. The motion resembles painting a semicircle on the mat with the back of their hand. Apply pressure progressively, giving your opponent time to recognize and tap to the submission.

Continue the arc until the opponent taps or you reach their maximum range of motion. Maintain hip pressure throughout to prevent escape attempts during the finish. If the opponent does not tap and you feel significant resistance in their shoulder, hold steady pressure rather than cranking further. Be prepared to release instantly upon any tap signal.

common_counters.counter: Arm straightening defense - opponent extends their trapped arm fully to prevent the figure-four grip
common_counters.your_response: Transition to kimura by circling your grip around their straightened wrist and attacking the opposite rotational direction. Alternatively, use your chest pressure to walk their elbow back to bent position before re-attempting the figure-four.

common_counters.counter: Gripping own belt or pants - opponent anchors their wrist to their body to resist the paint brush motion
common_counters.your_response: Maintain the figure-four grip and use your hip pressure to isolate the arm further. Peel their grip by driving your forearm into the gap between their hand and body. If the grip is too strong, threaten a transition to armbar to force them to release.

common_counters.counter: Bridge and roll during grip transition - opponent exploits the moment you release head control
common_counters.your_response: Anticipate the bridge by widening your base before releasing head control. If they bridge, ride it out with hip pressure and re-establish head control before attempting the transition again. Speed up the wrist capture to minimize the vulnerable window.

common_counters.counter: Turning into attacker to close distance and prevent rotation
common_counters.your_response: Their turn actually improves your angle for the americana by exposing more of their shoulder. Use the momentum of their turn to accelerate the paint brush motion. Maintain elbow pin throughout their rotation attempt.

common_errors.error: Releasing head control too early before securing wrist grip
common_errors.consequence: Opponent uses the free moment to establish frames, extract their trapped arm, or initiate bridge-and-roll escape that recovers guard position
common_errors.correction: Overlap the grip transition by beginning to slide your far hand toward the wrist while still maintaining head pressure. Only fully release head control when your hand is already on or near the wrist.

common_errors.error: Applying force with arms instead of body rotation during the paint brush finish
common_errors.consequence: Insufficient leverage to overcome opponent's shoulder strength, rapid fatigue in your arms, and telegraphed intention that allows opponent to brace and defend
common_errors.correction: Keep your arms as structural connectors only. Drive the paint brush motion by rotating your entire torso while keeping your hips heavy. The power comes from your core and body weight, not your biceps.

common_errors.error: Failing to pin the elbow firmly to the mat before applying rotational pressure
common_errors.consequence: The opponent can pull their elbow off the mat and toward their body, collapsing the submission angle and potentially extracting their arm entirely
common_errors.correction: Before threading the figure-four, use your near arm to press the elbow firmly into the mat. Maintain downward pressure on the elbow throughout the submission. The pinned elbow is the non-negotiable fulcrum.

common_errors.error: Sitting too upright during the submission attempt and losing chest connection
common_errors.consequence: Creates space for opponent to hip escape, turn into you, or generate bridge leverage that disrupts the entire submission sequence
common_errors.correction: Stay low with your chest pressing into the opponent's upper body throughout the entire sequence. Your hip pressure should remain constant against their ribcage even while transitioning grips.

common_errors.error: Rushing the submission with jerky or explosive force
common_errors.consequence: Risk of serious shoulder injury to your training partner, potential for losing the grip due to lack of control, and violation of safe training protocols
common_errors.correction: Apply the paint brush in a slow, controlled arc over 3-5 seconds minimum. Progressive pressure gives your opponent time to tap and gives you better control of the finishing mechanics.

common_errors.error: Positioning the figure-four grip too high on the opponent's hand instead of behind the wrist
common_errors.consequence: Opponent can slip their hand free through the gap, the rotational leverage is reduced, and the submission becomes a wrist lock rather than a shoulder lock
common_errors.correction: Place your forearm directly behind the opponent's wrist joint, ensuring contact across the full width of the wrist. The grip should control the forearm's rotation, not just the hand.

training_progressions.focus: Figure-four grip formation and wrist-to-elbow control
training_progressions.description: Partner lies flat with arm bent at 90 degrees. Practice transitioning from head control to wrist control, forming the figure-four, and pinning the elbow. No finishing pressure. 30 repetitions each side focusing on smooth grip transitions and proper forearm placement behind the wrist.

training_progressions.focus: Complete sequence from scarf hold to submission finish
training_progressions.description: From established scarf hold, execute the full americana sequence with a cooperative partner. Apply finishing pressure at 10-20% only. Focus on maintaining hip pressure throughout, smooth grip transitions, and slow controlled paint brush motion. 15 repetitions each side.

training_progressions.focus: Identifying and defeating common defensive responses
training_progressions.description: Partner provides specific defenses: arm straightening, belt grip, bridging during transition. Attacker practices appropriate responses for each counter. Build the if-then decision tree through repetition. 5 rounds of 3 minutes with increasing resistance.

training_progressions.focus: Applying the submission against full resistance from scarf hold
training_progressions.description: Begin in established scarf hold with full resistance. Attacker attempts americana while partner defends with all available tools. Chain to kimura, armbar, or positional transitions when americana is defended. 5 rounds of 3 minutes with 1-minute rest.

flashcards.question: What anatomical structure does the Americana from Scarf Hold primarily attack?
flashcards.answer: The Americana primarily attacks the glenohumeral joint (shoulder) by forcing external rotation beyond its safe range of motion. The rotational pressure stresses the rotator cuff muscles (supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor, subscapularis), the shoulder capsule, and the labrum. Secondary stress occurs at the AC joint when the arm is driven toward the mat.

flashcards.question: Your opponent begins straightening their arm as you transition from head control to wrist control - what adjustment prevents this defense?
flashcards.answer: Immediately abandon the americana attempt and transition to a kimura grip by circling around their straightened wrist to attack the opposite rotational direction. A straightened arm is the ideal setup for a kimura. Alternatively, use your chest pressure to collapse their extended arm back to bent position by walking your body weight over the elbow before re-attempting the figure-four. Never chase a straightening arm with americana mechanics.

trap: Keep chasing arm to lock americana

flashcards.question: What is the correct fulcrum point when finishing the Americana from Scarf Hold?
flashcards.answer: The pinned elbow serves as the fulcrum point. It must be pressed firmly against the mat by your near arm before any rotational pressure is applied. The elbow remains stationary while the wrist arcs toward the mat in the paint brush motion. Without a firmly pinned elbow, the opponent can pull their arm toward their body and collapse the submission angle entirely, negating your leverage advantage.

flashcards.question: You have the figure-four secured but the opponent is resisting the paint brush by gripping their own belt - what do you do?
flashcards.answer: Maintain your figure-four grip and increase hip pressure to further isolate the arm. Use your forearm to peel their grip by driving into the gap between their hand and their belt or waistband. If the grip is too strong to break directly, threaten a transition to armbar by beginning to swing your leg over their head, which forces them to release the belt grip to defend the new threat. Return to the americana once their grip breaks.

flashcards.question: How does the perpendicular angle of Scarf Hold change the Americana finishing mechanics compared to mount?
flashcards.answer: The perpendicular angle allows you to use full torso rotation to drive the paint brush motion rather than relying primarily on arm strength as in mount. Your body weight drives through the hip into their ribcage at a 90-degree angle, preventing the opponent from bridging effectively. The scarf hold also provides natural wrist proximity through the existing head-and-arm control, making the grip transition shorter and more efficient than from mount where you must first isolate the arm.

trap: Rely on arm strength like mount

flashcards.question: Your opponent bridges explosively during your grip transition from head control to wrist capture - how do you maintain control?
flashcards.answer: Widen your base immediately by extending your back leg further behind you and dropping your hip weight lower against their ribcage. Ride the bridge by staying connected through chest pressure rather than posting away. If the bridge is strong enough to create space, abandon the americana attempt and re-establish head control first. Only re-attempt the grip transition when you have consolidated heavy hip pressure and confirmed your base can absorb their bridge.

flashcards.question: What are the key safety considerations when applying the Americana from Scarf Hold in training?
flashcards.answer: Apply pressure slowly and progressively over 3-5 seconds minimum. Never jerk, spike, or use sudden rotational force on the shoulder. In drilling, use 10-20% pressure maximum. Always ensure your opponent has clear access to tap with their free hand. Stop immediately at any sign of discomfort without waiting for a formal tap. Never practice repeatedly on the same shoulder in one session. Be especially cautious with training partners who have existing shoulder injuries.

plausible: Full pressure with quick taps ok

flashcards.question: How should you release the Americana from Scarf Hold after your opponent taps?
flashcards.answer: Immediately stop all rotational pressure on the shoulder. Release the figure-four grip on the wrist. Carefully lower the arm back to a neutral position without dropping it suddenly, as the shoulder may already be stressed. Release all control of the elbow and allow your opponent to move freely. Verbally check with your partner to confirm they are okay. If they indicate any pain, encourage them to keep the shoulder mobile and seek medical attention if pain persists.

flashcards.question: At what point during the Americana application is the submission considered past the point of no escape?
flashcards.answer: The point of no escape occurs once the figure-four grip is fully locked with the elbow pinned to the mat and the attacker's hip pressure prevents any torso rotation. At this stage, the defender cannot straighten their arm, grip their belt, or bridge effectively. The only remaining option is to tap. This is why early recognition and defense before the figure-four is secured is critical for the defender, and why the attacker must apply progressive pressure once reaching this control threshold.

flashcards.question: What submission chain options exist when the Americana from Scarf Hold is partially defended?
flashcards.answer: If the opponent straightens their arm, transition to kimura by circling the grip to attack opposite rotation. If they turn into you to close the angle, switch to arm triangle by threading your arm around their neck and trapped arm. If they push on your head with their far arm, attack that arm with a far-side armbar or transition to north-south for additional submission options. The scarf hold americana is most effective as part of a chain rather than as an isolated attack.
flashcards.answer_line: Chain to kimura or arm triangle

defender.name: from Scarf Hold Position Defender
defender.description: Defend against the Americana from Scarf Hold. Recognition cues, arm straightening defense, grip fighting techniques, and escape timing from kesa gatame.
defender.overview: Defending the Americana from Scarf Hold requires immediate recognition of the grip transition and proactive arm protection before the figure-four is locked. The scarf hold's perpendicular angle makes this americana variant particularly dangerous because the attacker maintains crushing chest pressure throughout the submission attempt, limiting your defensive mobility. Your primary weapons are arm straightening to prevent the figure-four, grip fighting to deny wrist control, and exploiting the attacker's weight shift during the submission attempt to create escape opportunities. Early defense is essential because once the figure-four is secured with your elbow pinned, the submission is nearly impossible to escape.
key_principles: Recognize the grip transition immediately - the moment the attacker releases head control to grab your wrist is your primary defensive window
Straighten your trapped arm aggressively the instant you feel wrist control being established to prevent the figure-four formation
Keep your elbow tight to your body and off the mat to deny the fulcrum point the attacker needs for the paint brush finish
Use the attacker's grip transition as an escape opportunity since they temporarily sacrifice head control for submission setup
Fight grips proactively by stripping wrist control before the figure-four is locked rather than trying to escape after
Maintain composure under chest pressure and work systematically through defensive priorities rather than panicking
recognition_cues: Attacker releases head control with their far arm and begins sliding their hand toward your near-side wrist or forearm
Attacker increases hip pressure and adjusts their perpendicular angle slightly toward your head, loading weight over your shoulder
Attacker's near arm shifts from general arm control to specifically pressing your elbow toward the mat
You feel your forearm being pushed flat against the mat with the back of your hand facing down

defensive_options.action: Straighten trapped arm and grip your own thigh or belt to anchor
defensive_options.when_to_use: As soon as you feel the attacker transitioning to wrist control, before the figure-four is locked
defensive_options.if_successful: Denies the figure-four grip entirely, forcing attacker to abandon americana or transition to kimura
defensive_options.risk: Straightening the arm may expose you to kimura attack in the opposite rotational direction

defensive_options.action: Bridge and turn into attacker during their grip transition window
defensive_options.when_to_use: During the 1-2 second window when attacker has released head control but not yet secured the figure-four
defensive_options.if_successful: Recover closed guard or half guard as the attacker loses perpendicular positioning during the scramble
defensive_options.risk: If bridge is poorly timed, attacker may secure wrist control during your bridge and finish from an even stronger angle

defensive_options.action: Strip wrist grip by pulling elbow tight to body and rotating forearm
defensive_options.when_to_use: When attacker has grabbed your wrist but has not yet threaded the figure-four behind it
defensive_options.if_successful: Breaks the attacker's wrist control and forces them to restart the submission setup or return to standard scarf hold
defensive_options.risk: Requires precise timing and grip strength; if unsuccessful, the attacker may tighten control further

defensive_options.action: Frame on attacker's hip and shrimp to create distance during submission attempt
defensive_options.when_to_use: When attacker commits weight forward to set up the americana and creates slight space near your hips
defensive_options.if_successful: Create enough distance to recover guard position while attacker is focused on the submission rather than maintaining position
defensive_options.risk: Difficult to execute against a well-positioned attacker; may not create enough space if hip pressure is maintained

escape_paths: Straighten arm and anchor grip to thigh or belt, then work standard scarf hold escape progressions (bridge-and-roll or ghost escape)
Bridge explosively during the grip transition window when attacker releases head control, turning into them to recover closed guard or half guard
Strip wrist control before figure-four is locked, then immediately chain into backdoor escape to turtle position

favorable_outcomes.how: Exploit the attacker's grip transition by bridging when they release head control. Turn into the attacker and use the momentum to recover guard as their perpendicular position breaks down during the scramble.
Successfully defend the americana through arm straightening or grip stripping, returning to standard scarf hold bottom position where you can work primary escape sequences.

common_errors.error: Bending the trapped arm when feeling wrist control being established
common_errors.consequence: Creates the perfect 90-degree angle the attacker needs to lock the figure-four and pin your elbow as the fulcrum, making the americana nearly impossible to escape
common_errors.correction: The instant you feel wrist control, aggressively straighten your arm by driving your hand toward your feet. A straight arm cannot be figure-foured. Even partial straightening makes the submission significantly harder to finish.

common_errors.error: Waiting until the figure-four is locked before attempting defense
common_errors.consequence: Once the figure-four is secured with your elbow pinned, escape success rate drops to near zero. The attacker has full mechanical advantage and you have almost no defensive leverage.
common_errors.correction: Defend at the earliest possible moment - during the grip transition. Every fraction of a second you wait makes defense exponentially harder. The defensive window closes rapidly once the attacker begins threading the figure-four.

common_errors.error: Bridging without addressing the arm control first
common_errors.consequence: The bridge may create space but your trapped arm remains controlled, allowing the attacker to finish the americana from a modified angle or use your bridge to tighten their position
common_errors.correction: Address arm control simultaneously with your bridge. Strip the wrist grip or straighten your arm as you bridge, combining defensive actions rather than sequencing them. A bridge alone does not solve the arm isolation problem.

common_errors.error: Panicking under chest pressure and making explosive but untimed escape attempts
common_errors.consequence: Rapid energy depletion that leaves you unable to mount effective defense when genuine escape windows appear. The attacker simply waits for you to exhaust yourself before finishing.
common_errors.correction: Accept the discomfort of chest pressure and focus on controlled breathing. Save explosive energy for precise moments when the attacker transitions grips. Methodical defense is far more effective than panicked struggling.

flashcards.question: How do you recognize the Americana from Scarf Hold is being set up?
flashcards.answer: The primary recognition cue is the attacker releasing head control with their far arm and sliding it toward your near-side wrist. You will also feel increased hip pressure as they load weight over your shoulder, and their near arm will begin pressing your elbow specifically toward the mat. The tactile cue of your forearm being flattened against the mat with your hand palm-up confirms the americana setup is in progress.
flashcards.answer_line: Far arm slides to your wrist

trap: Ignore it, it's just a grip

flashcards.question: What is the safest way to tap to the Americana from Scarf Hold to prevent injury?
flashcards.answer: Tap early and clearly before you feel sharp pain in the shoulder. Use your free hand to tap firmly on the attacker's body or the mat at least twice. If your free hand is obstructed, tap the mat with your foot or verbalize 'tap' loudly. Do not try to be tough and ride through shoulder pressure - the americana applies force to the rotator cuff and labrum which can tear without warning. Tap the moment you feel the shoulder reaching its end range of comfortable motion.

flashcards.question: What defensive options are available when the figure-four grip is partially locked?
flashcards.answer: If the figure-four is partially but not fully locked, aggressively strip the grip by pulling your elbow tight to your ribs and rotating your forearm to break the attacker's hand position. Bridge simultaneously to disrupt their base and create enough movement to dislodge the incomplete grip. If the grip is nearly complete, prioritize straightening your arm before the last connection is made, as a straight arm cannot be effectively attacked with americana mechanics.
flashcards.answer_line: Strip grip, pull elbow to ribs

plausible: Wait and see if it locks

flashcards.question: Your opponent has pinned your elbow and is beginning the paint brush motion - what is your last viable defense?
flashcards.answer: At this late stage, your options are extremely limited. Grip your own thigh, belt, or waistband with maximum strength to anchor your wrist and resist the paint brush motion. Simultaneously bridge toward the attacker to disrupt their rotational angle. If you cannot stop the progression, tap immediately rather than risking shoulder injury. Once the elbow is pinned and the paint brush begins, the submission is mechanically sound and fighting through it risks serious rotator cuff or labral damage.
flashcards.answer_line: Anchor wrist to belt or thigh

trap: Fight the rotation with arm strength

flashcards.question: When should you prioritize tapping rather than continuing escape attempts against the Americana?
flashcards.answer: Tap immediately if you feel sharp pain in the shoulder joint, if your arm is being rotated beyond its comfortable range and you cannot stop the progression, if the figure-four is fully locked with your elbow pinned and you have no grip anchor, or if you feel a popping or clicking sensation in the shoulder. In training, err heavily toward tapping early. A shoulder injury can sideline you for months. No training round is worth a torn rotator cuff or dislocated shoulder.
flashcards.answer_line: At sharp pain or full lock

training_progressions.focus: Identifying americana setup cues and immediate arm straightening response
training_progressions.description: Partner establishes scarf hold and slowly transitions toward americana setup. Defender focuses on recognizing the grip transition moment and immediately straightening their arm. No full submissions applied. 20 repetitions focusing purely on recognition speed and arm straightening reflex.

training_progressions.focus: Stripping wrist control and maintaining arm position under increasing resistance
training_progressions.description: Partner attempts to secure wrist control with moderate pressure. Defender practices stripping grips, anchoring to belt or thigh, and maintaining straight arm position. Build to 70% resistance over 10 repetitions each side. Focus on timing grip strips before figure-four completion.

training_progressions.focus: Combining americana defense with scarf hold escape sequences
training_progressions.description: Partner attempts full americana from scarf hold at progressive resistance levels. Defender chains americana defense directly into escape attempts - bridge during grip transition, ghost escape when arm control is disrupted, guard recovery when space is created. 5 rounds of 3 minutes with full resistance.
